stem: An operations coordinator uploads a 40-page supplier contract and asks Claude to summarize the key obligations, renewal dates, and penalty clauses. The summary reads fluently and is well organized. What should the coordinator do first before relying on it?

options.text: Check the summary for grammar, consistent formatting and a professional tone so it is ready to circulate to the procurement team without further editing.
options.why: Polish is not accuracy. A fluent, well-formatted summary can still omit a penalty clause or misstate a date.

options.text: Ask Claude whether the summary is complete and accurate, and accept it if Claude confirms that nothing important was left out.
options.why: Claude's own assessment of its output is not an independent check; it will usually affirm what it just wrote.

options.text: Check that every element she asked for is present and that each one matches the contract text.
options.why: Completeness is judged against what was asked (obligations, renewal dates, penalties) and accuracy against the primary source, not against how confident the summary sounds.

options.text: Check that the summary is roughly one page long, since that is the usual length for a contract of this size.
options.why: Length says nothing about whether the right clauses were captured or whether the figures are correct.

explanation: Evaluating a Claude output means checking it on two axes: completeness against the original ask (did it cover everything requested?) and accuracy against the source (does each claim match the document?). Fluency, formatting, and Claude's self-assessment are not evidence of either.
reference: Claude Help Center — Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses

stem: A finance analyst uploads a 60-page annual report PDF and asks Claude for a table of revenue and operating margin for each of the company's 8 business units. Claude returns a neat table with revenue for all 8 units and margins for 5, noting that margins were "not reported" for the other 3. The figures look plausible. What is the most reliable way to evaluate this output?

options.text: List the 16 requested values (8 units x 2 metrics) and confirm each one, including the 3 "not reported" margins, against the page of the report where it should appear.
options.why: A checklist derived from the ask exposes gaps, and tracing each value to its page catches both wrong figures and false claims that data is missing (Claude may simply have not found page 47).

options.text: Check that the 8 revenue figures add up to the group revenue total printed on the first page of the report, and accept the whole table if they reconcile, since a correct total implies correct components.
options.why: A reconciled total is a useful sanity check on one column, but it says nothing about the margins or about whether the three "missing" values really are absent from the report.

options.text: Ask Claude in the same chat whether any figures are missing or wrong, and act on its answer.
options.why: Claude reviewing its own table in the same conversation tends to confirm it; this is not an independent completeness check.

options.text: Accept the table because the figures are formatted consistently and fall in a realistic range for the industry.
options.why: Plausibility and clean formatting are exactly what makes a wrong number dangerous; realism is not verification.

explanation: Completeness is measured against the original request, so enumerate what was asked and tick each item off against the source. Claims that data is "not reported" are themselves claims to verify; a long PDF is a common place for Claude to miss a section rather than the data being absent.
reference: Claude Help Center — Upload files to Claude; Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations

stem: An HR manager uploads the company's current leave policy and asks Claude to draft a new parental-leave section that meets three requirements: 12 weeks paid, applies equally to adoptive parents, and eligibility after 6 months of service. Claude returns a polished draft with an eligibility table and several figures. Which two checks best evaluate the draft for accuracy and completeness? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run the draft through a readability tool and confirm it scores at or below a grade-10 reading level.
options.why: Readability is a refinement concern for the audience; it does not tell the manager whether the policy says the right things.

options.text: Confirm that each of the three stated requirements appears in the draft and is stated exactly as specified (12 weeks paid, adoptive parents included, 6-month eligibility).
options.why: Completeness is checked against the original ask; a draft that silently changes 6 months to 12, or omits adoptive parents, fails even if it reads well.

options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence in the draft from 1 to 10 and proceed if it scores 8 or higher.
options.why: Self-rated confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal; the exam guide is explicit that it should not drive a decision to use an output.

options.text: For every figure or rule in the draft that was not in the three requirements, ask Claude to point to the passage of the uploaded policy it came from, and remove anything it cannot source.
options.why: Drafts often absorb generic industry norms (notice periods, accrual rules) that were never in the company's policy; tracing each extra detail to the source separates grounded content from invented content.

options.text: Compare the draft against three competitors' public parental-leave policies to see whether it is competitive.
options.why: Benchmarking may be useful for policy design, but it is not an accuracy check of this draft against this company's requirements and documents.

explanation: Evaluate on two axes: every stated requirement must be present and exact (completeness against the ask), and every additional detail must trace to the provided source (accuracy against the source). Readability, confidence ratings and benchmarking do not answer either question.
reference: Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations (verify with citations)

stem: A compliance officer asks Claude to condense a 90-page regulatory guidance document into a list of the firm's 10 key obligations, which will be circulated to department heads as the basis for control changes. She spot-checks 3 of the 10 against the document and all 3 are correct. She has one hour before the list is due. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Circulate the list now, since a 3-for-3 spot check on a random sample gives reasonable statistical confidence that the remaining 7 obligations are also correctly stated.
options.why: Three correct items say little about the other seven, and nothing about obligations that were left out entirely; the downstream use (control changes) makes an omission costly.

options.text: Re-run the same request in a fresh chat with the same document attached, compare the two lists side by side, and circulate the original if the two versions broadly agree on the 10 obligations.
options.why: Consistency between two runs can flag hallucinations, but two runs can share the same omission; it is not a check against the source document.

options.text: Ask Claude in the same chat to list any obligations it may have omitted from the guidance, add those to the list, and circulate the expanded version.
options.why: Asking the model what it missed relies on the same process that produced the gap; it is not a substitute for checking the source.

options.text: Have Claude cite the section and quoted passage for each of the 10, verify all 10 against the document, and scan the document's headings for topics the list omits.
options.why: Ten cited claims are verifiable within the hour; verifying each against the source checks accuracy, and scanning the headings checks completeness in the direction a spot check cannot (what was left out).

explanation: A spot check only estimates the error rate of what is present; it cannot detect omissions. When the list is short enough to verify fully and the consequences are material, ask Claude to cite the passage for each claim, verify every one, and check the source for topics the output does not mention.
reference: Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations (verify with citations); CCAO-F Exam Guide sample 1

stem: A market researcher uploads a CSV of 200 survey responses in which respondents could tick any number of complaint categories, and asks Claude for the top five complaints with the percentage of respondents citing each. Claude returns five categories whose percentages sum to exactly 100%, and the accompanying text refers to "the 180 respondents". The researcher wants to use the figures in a client presentation. What is the correct reading of this output, and what should she do?

options.text: The percentages are fine because the difference between 200 and 180 is probably blank rows that Claude excluded; rescale the five figures to reflect multi-select and use them.
options.why: This guesses at the reason for both anomalies and then manually adjusts numbers whose derivation is unknown, producing figures nobody can defend to the client.

options.text: Two inconsistencies (multi-select percentages summing to 100%, an unexplained respondent count) suggest the figures were estimated, not computed; have Claude show its method, produce real counts with its data analysis tool, and reconcile 200 versus 180 first.
options.why: Internal inconsistency is a hallucination signal; the fix is to make the computation explicit and traceable to the data, then resolve the discrepancy, rather than to patch the numbers.

options.text: Ask Claude to redo the analysis with the instruction "be precise and double-check your numbers before answering", and use the second set of figures if they look more reasonable than the first.
options.why: An exhortation to be accurate does not change how the numbers were produced; without a visible method the second set is as unverifiable as the first.

options.text: Use the figures as directional only and label the slide "approximate", since exact percentages rarely matter in a top-five ranking.
options.why: The inconsistencies cast doubt on the ranking itself, not just the decimal places; a category could be in the top five only because of an error.

explanation: Numbers that contradict each other or the structure of the data (multi-select percentages summing to 100%, a respondent count that changed) are evidence the model estimated rather than computed. Make the method visible, have the counts computed from the data, and reconcile every discrepancy before a figure leaves the building.
reference: Claude Help Center — Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses; Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations

stem: A paralegal asks Claude, in a chat with web search turned off, for case law supporting a client's position. Claude returns three cases, each with party names, a year, a court, and a reporter citation. What should the paralegal recognize about this output?

options.text: Because the citations include reporter volumes, page numbers and courts, they must have been drawn from real records and can be quoted in a filing after a quick format check.
options.why: The precise format is the hallmark of a fabricated citation; models generate the format from patterns, not from a database lookup.

options.text: The first case is likely reliable and the later ones less so, since Claude lists its strongest sources first.
options.why: There is no such ordering rule; any or all of the cases may be invented, and position in the list carries no information about reliability.

options.text: Asking Claude to confirm that each case is real will resolve any doubt before they are used.
options.why: Asking the model to confirm its own citation in the same conversation typically produces a confident yes; it is not verification.

options.text: Precise-looking citations can be fabricated; each case must be located and read in a legal database before use.
options.why: Invented citations are a classic hallucination. The only reliable check is retrieving each cited source from an authoritative database.

explanation: Hallucinations often look most convincing when they are most specific: named cases, reporter citations, section numbers. Specificity is not evidence. Treat every citation as unverified until the source is retrieved and read.
reference: Claude Help Center — Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses

stem: A communications manager, working in a chat with web search off, asks Claude to draft a press note that references "the industry survey published last month". Claude's draft names a report title, states that 63.4% of respondents plan to increase spending, and quotes a sentence from the report's foreword. Which feature of the draft is the strongest hallucination red flag?

options.text: The draft uses a formal, corporate tone that differs noticeably from the manager's usual press notes, which suggests Claude was not working from her earlier examples.
options.why: Tone is a refinement issue; it does not bear on whether the facts are real.

options.text: Claude is asserting specific figures and a quotation from a recent document it had no way to see, since no source was provided.
options.why: Confident detail about a recent event, produced with no web search and no uploaded document, cannot be grounded in anything; the title, statistic and quote should all be presumed invented until sourced.

options.text: The statistic is expressed to one decimal place, which is unusual for a press note and suggests the figure was copied from a table rather than summarized.
options.why: Spurious precision is a secondary signal, but the fundamental problem is that Claude had no access to the report at all.

options.text: The draft does not include a hyperlink to the report, so readers cannot click through to the original source.
options.why: A link would not make the claims true; Claude can generate plausible-looking links that do not work.

explanation: Claude's training has a cutoff and, without web search or an uploaded file, it has no way to know the contents of a recent report. Confident specifics about recent events, fabricated quotes and invented titles are textbook hallucinations; the manager should upload the report or run a search and require citations.
reference: Claude Help Center — How up to date is Claude's training data; Claude is producing links that don't work

stem: A market analyst reviews a competitive-landscape summary Claude produced from a mix of uploaded reports and web search. Which three features of the summary should be treated as red flags for hallucination or inconsistency? (Choose three.)

options.text: A quotation attributed by name to a competitor's CEO, with no source cited anywhere in the summary.
options.why: Fabricated quotes attributed to real people are a common hallucination and are reputationally dangerous if repeated.

options.text: A closing section titled "Gaps and limitations" that lists questions the sources did not answer.
options.why: Acknowledging what is unknown is a sign of a well-grounded output, not a red flag; Anthropic's guidance encourages letting Claude say it does not know.

options.text: The market is described as growing 12% in one section and as contracting in a later section, with no explanation.
options.why: An internal contradiction means at least one statement is wrong; both must be traced to sources before either is used.

options.text: Several claims are hedged with phrases such as "reports suggest" and "appears to".
options.why: Hedging signals appropriate uncertainty; it is the confident, unhedged specifics that deserve the most scrutiny.

options.text: A market-share figure given to one decimal place for a private company, with no citation.
options.why: Precise-sounding numbers for data that is rarely public, and with no source, are characteristic of invented statistics.

options.text: Claude states that it could not find pricing data for one region and left that cell blank.
options.why: Leaving a gap rather than filling it with a guess is the behaviour you want; it is the opposite of a hallucination.

explanation: Hallucination red flags include unsourced quotes attributed to named people, precise numbers with no citation (especially for data that is not public), and statements that contradict each other. Hedging, acknowledged gaps and stated limitations are signs of a grounded output rather than problems.
reference: Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations; Claude Help Center — Using Research on Claude.ai

stem: An HR business partner pastes 40 anonymized candidate summaries for a customer-support lead role and asks Claude to rank them. The role's stated criteria are 3+ years of frontline support experience and experience coaching a team. In Claude's top 10, nine mention a prestigious university and eight mention a large well-known employer, while several candidates with strong coaching experience at small companies rank near the bottom. What is the best diagnosis and response?

options.text: The ranking is fair because the summaries were anonymized before upload, so no protected characteristic could have influenced it; the prestige pattern simply reflects stronger candidates.
options.why: Removing names does not remove proxies; institution prestige and employer size can act as proxies that skew results away from the actual criteria.

options.text: Ask Claude directly whether its ranking was influenced by university or employer prestige and, if it says the ranking was based only on the criteria, use it to shortlist.
options.why: The model cannot reliably audit its own weighting, and a reassuring answer is not evidence.

options.text: The ranking weights prestige proxies that are not in the criteria; re-run it with an explicit rubric for the stated criteria only, require quoted evidence for each score, and keep the shortlist decision with a human.
options.why: Skewed framing is diagnosed by comparing what the output rewards with what was asked; the remedy is explicit criteria, traceable evidence and a human decision, not trust in the first ranking.

options.text: Accept the ranking because Claude produced the same order when the request was run a second time.
options.why: Consistency shows the skew is systematic, not that it is correct; a repeatable bias is still a bias.

explanation: Bias in an output shows up as a pattern of favouring attributes that were not in the stated criteria. Anonymization does not remove proxies. Make the criteria explicit, require evidence for each score, and treat the model's ranking as input to a human decision, never as the decision itself.
reference: Anthropic — Evaluating and mitigating discrimination in language model decisions

stem: A public-sector procurement officer asks Claude to compare two vendor proposals (both uploaded) and recommend one. Claude recommends Vendor A. In the narrative, Vendor B's price is described as "aggressive" and Vendor A's as "competitive", although a table earlier in the response shows B's total is 8% lower. The table lists A's implementation time as 6 months, but the conclusion says A can "deliver in 4 months". The officer must document a defensible decision. Which action addresses both problems?

options.text: Discard the recommendation, ask Claude for a neutral side-by-side against the tender's published scoring criteria with each figure cited to a page of the proposals, then check every cited figure before scoring.
options.why: The loaded adjectives indicate skewed framing and the 6-versus-4-month conflict indicates an unreliable fact; both are fixed by re-anchoring on explicit criteria with traceable, human-verified figures rather than on Claude's narrative.

options.text: Ask Claude to correct the implementation timeline to 6 months and re-issue the recommendation with the corrected figure.
options.why: Patching one visible error leaves the skewed framing intact, and other figures in the narrative may be equally unreliable.

options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite the analysis recommending Vendor B instead, since B's total price is lower and the framing was unfair to B.
options.why: Swapping the conclusion substitutes one unexamined framing for another; price is only one of the tender's criteria.

options.text: Run the comparison twice more in fresh chats and go with whichever vendor is recommended in at least two of the three runs.
options.why: Majority voting across runs does not verify any figure against the proposals and can reproduce the same framing three times.

explanation: Two signals appeared together: evaluative language inconsistent with the numbers (skewed framing) and a figure that contradicts the response's own table (inconsistency). Neither is fixed by patching or re-running; re-anchor on explicit criteria, require cited figures, and verify them against the primary documents before deciding.
reference: Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations (verify with citations); CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2

stem: A retail operations analyst asks Claude for a slide outline on returns management. One bullet states that the industry-average online return rate is 24.6%. She wants to keep the figure in the deck. What is the most appropriate way to validate it?

options.text: Ask Claude "Are you sure about 24.6%?" in the same chat and keep the figure if Claude confirms it and explains where it comes from.
options.why: A model asked to confirm its own claim will usually do so; this is not verification.

options.text: Find the primary source, confirm the number, its date and what it measures, and cite that source on the slide.
options.why: Statistics are validated against the original publication, which also reveals the context (year, market, definition of "return") that decides whether the number fits the slide.

options.text: Ask Claude to provide the figure to two decimal places along with the year it applies to, which shows it is drawing on real data.
options.why: Extra precision is trivially generated and is, if anything, a hallucination signal rather than evidence.

options.text: Search for the number online and keep it if several websites and blog posts repeat the same 24.6% value.
options.why: Repetition across secondary sites often traces back to a single misquoted or outdated origin; the check is the primary source, not the number of echoes.

explanation: Fact-checking a statistic means finding the primary source and confirming the number, its date and its definition. Neither the model's confirmation, its precision, nor the number of secondary sites repeating it is a substitute.
reference: Claude Help Center — Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses

stem: A project manager uploads a 120-page vendor master services agreement to a Project and asks Claude whether the contract allows termination for convenience. Claude answers that it does, with 60 days' notice, "under the termination clause". Which validation technique best confirms the answer?

options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence in the answer on a scale of 1 to 10 and accept the answer if the rating is 8 or higher.
options.why: Self-rated confidence is not a reliable indicator of accuracy; the exam guide calls this out specifically.

options.text: Ask Claude in the same chat "Can you confirm that clause really exists and says 60 days?" and accept the answer if Claude says yes.
options.why: A leading question in the same conversation invites the model to reaffirm what it already said; it does not add evidence.

options.text: Ask Claude to quote the exact passage with its section and page, then open that page in the PDF and read the clause.
options.why: Grounding the claim in a word-for-word quote with a location makes it auditable, and reading the passage in the source is the actual verification.

options.text: Ask Claude to summarize the whole termination section again in more detail and compare the two summaries for consistency.
options.why: Comparing two model-generated summaries checks consistency, not truth; both can restate the same misreading.

explanation: For claims drawn from a provided document, ask Claude to quote the passage it relied on and where it is, then verify against the document. Direct quotes and citations make outputs auditable; confidence ratings and self-confirmation do not.
reference: Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations (use direct quotes, verify with citations)

stem: A market researcher used Research mode to produce a briefing on electric-vehicle adoption in three countries. The briefing contains six statistics; four carry citation links and two do not. Which two steps are appropriate fact-checking practice before the briefing goes to a client? (Choose two.)

options.text: Open each cited source and confirm that the figure, its year and the population it describes match what the briefing says.
options.why: A citation is a pointer, not proof; the source can be misread, out of date, or about a different population, so the researcher must check the claim against it.

options.text: Treat the four figures with citation links as verified, since Research mode attaches sources automatically.
options.why: Research citations are designed to be easy to check, not to replace checking; a linked source may not say what the summary claims.

options.text: Ask Claude to add a confidence score next to each statistic and drop any below 80%.
options.why: Self-reported confidence does not track accuracy and would give false comfort on the figures that pass.

options.text: For the two unsourced figures, run a fresh search or research query to find a primary source, and remove any figure for which none can be found.
options.why: Cross-checking with a second query and requiring a source, with removal as the default when none exists, follows Anthropic's guidance to retract claims that cannot be supported.

options.text: Reword the two unsourced statistics as approximations ("roughly a fifth") so that precision is not implied.
options.why: Softening the wording does not make an unverified number true; a vague version of a fabricated statistic is still fabricated.

explanation: Citations make claims checkable but do not verify them; the researcher still opens the source and compares. Unsourced claims get a second, independent attempt at sourcing and are removed if that fails. Confidence scores and softer wording do not change whether a figure is correct.
reference: Claude Help Center — Using Research on Claude.ai; Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations

stem: A finance analyst uploads a spreadsheet of five years of regional sales and asks Claude to calculate the compound annual growth rate for each region. Claude reports 14.2% for the largest region, which will appear in a board deck. The analyst is fluent in spreadsheets and has 20 minutes. Which validation approach best fits?

options.text: Ask Claude to explain its reasoning step by step and accept the figure if the logic sounds right.
options.why: A sound-looking explanation can accompany a wrong number; reasoning review helps find errors but is not an independent computation.

options.text: Re-run the request in a new chat and accept the figure if the two results match.
options.why: Agreement between runs can still reflect the same wrong input cells or the same period assumption; it is consistency, not correctness.

options.text: Trust the figure because Claude used its data analysis tool, which executes real calculations on the uploaded file rather than estimating from the text.
options.why: Code execution removes arithmetic error but not choice-of-input error (wrong column, wrong start year, currency mix); the calculation still needs an independent check.

options.text: Ask Claude which cells and years it used, then recompute the growth rate in the spreadsheet with a formula and compare.
options.why: An independent recomputation from the source data, using the inputs Claude says it used, is the only option that verifies both the arithmetic and the assumptions in the time available.

explanation: When the person can independently recompute a figure from the primary data, that is the strongest validation: it checks the arithmetic and the inputs. Re-running, reasoning walkthroughs and tool-based execution each leave a class of error unchecked.
reference: Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations (chain-of-thought and best-of-N verification); Claude Help Center — Create and edit files with Claude

stem: A customer-service team lead, who is not a lawyer, uses Claude to draft a reply to a customer disputing a cancellation fee. The draft states that a named section of the national consumer-protection statute "permits the fee provided it was disclosed at sign-up". The reply will go to the customer today. Which validation approach is correct?

options.text: Turn on web search and ask Claude in the same chat to confirm the section number; keep the citation if Claude finds the statute.
options.why: Finding the statute confirms it exists, not that the section says what the draft claims; and the model is again grading its own claim.

options.text: Ask the same question in a second chat and, if the second answer cites the same section, treat the citation as validated.
options.why: Two model runs can share the same error; a cross-check adds evidence but is not a primary source, and the interpretation still needs a qualified reader.

options.text: Open the section on the official legislation site and compare it to the claim; because judging whether it permits the fee is a legal interpretation he cannot make, remove the citation or have legal confirm it before sending.
options.why: Verifying against the primary source catches an invented or misnumbered section, and recognizing that the remaining question is one of legal interpretation beyond his competence routes it to the right reviewer.

options.text: Use Research mode to produce a report on the statute with citations, and rely on its citations to support the reply.
options.why: Research is a good way to find sources, but its citations still have to be read, and reading a statute for legal effect is not something the team lead can validate alone.

explanation: Fact-checking has two parts: does the cited source exist and say what is claimed (verify against the primary text), and is the claim's interpretation something the checker is competent to judge (if not, escalate). A legal citation in a customer-facing message fails safe: remove it or get it confirmed by legal.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide sample 1; Claude Help Center — Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses

stem: A team assistant uses Claude for several small tasks in one afternoon. Which of the following outputs most clearly requires human review before it is used?

options.text: A list of ten brainstormed themes for the team's off-site, to be discussed and narrowed down by the whole team at the next stand-up.
options.why: Brainstorm output is low-stakes and will be discussed and filtered by the team anyway; errors have no consequence.

options.text: A draft reply to a customer's formal complaint about a billing error, to be sent from the support address.
options.why: External, customer-facing communication about money carries reputational and possibly legal consequences, so a person must review before it leaves the company.

options.text: A rewording of the assistant's own Slack message to sound friendlier before she posts it to the internal team channel.
options.why: The assistant wrote the original, knows what it should say, and the audience is internal; a quick read-through is enough.

options.text: A conversion of the assistant's meeting notes into a to-do list for herself.
options.why: The output is for her own use and she can correct it as she works; there is no downstream consequence.

explanation: Human review is required when an output is external, financial, legal, regulated, irreversible, or beyond what the person can verify. A customer-facing reply about a billing error ticks several of those boxes; internal notes and brainstorms do not.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2 (Determine when human review is required)

stem: An operations manager at an outpatient clinic uses Claude to turn a physician's bullet points into plain-language after-procedure instructions for patients. The draft is clear and reads correctly to her. What should happen before it is given to patients?

options.text: A clinician reviews and approves the medical content, regardless of how accurate the draft appears to the manager.
options.why: Medical guidance for patients is a high-consequence output that the manager is not qualified to verify; a qualified human must sign off.

options.text: The manager proofreads for grammar and formatting and distributes it, since the physician's bullets were the source.
options.why: Rephrasing can change meaning (a dose, a timing, an exception); the source being correct does not make the rewrite correct.

options.text: The manager asks Claude to double-check the instructions for medical accuracy and distributes them if no issues are found.
options.why: Claude checking its own medical output is not clinical review and does not transfer accountability to a qualified person.

options.text: Add a footer stating "Generated with AI assistance" so patients know to confirm anything unclear with their doctor.
options.why: A disclaimer does not make the content safe and shifts the burden to patients; the review has to happen before distribution.

explanation: Outputs in medical, legal, financial or regulated domains that reach an external audience require review by a qualified human, not just by the person who prompted. Reading well is not a substitute, and neither disclaimers nor self-checks by the model are.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2; Claude Help Center — Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses

stem: An HR operations team lists the tasks it plans to hand to Claude this quarter. Which two tasks produce outputs that require a qualified human to review before the output is acted on? (Choose two.)

options.text: Summarizing a recorded team meeting for the eight people who attended it.
options.why: The audience was present and can spot errors; the summary is low-risk and self-correcting.

options.text: Drafting a termination letter for an employee, based on the uploaded disciplinary policy.
options.why: Termination is legally sensitive and effectively irreversible; the letter must be reviewed by HR leadership and, typically, legal before it is issued.

options.text: Calculating annual bonus payouts for 120 employees from an uploaded spreadsheet of targets and results.
options.why: Financial outputs that trigger payments are high-consequence and hard to reverse; a person must verify the figures against the plan rules before payroll runs.

options.text: Suggesting five subject lines for the internal monthly newsletter.
options.why: Low stakes and internal; the editor picks one and any weak option is simply ignored.

options.text: Reformatting an existing onboarding checklist from paragraphs into a bulleted list.
options.why: A format change of existing content carries little risk, and the owner can glance over it as they use it.

explanation: The triggers for mandatory human review are consequence and reversibility: legal exposure, money moving, regulated content, external audiences, and anything the requester cannot verify alone. Formatting, brainstorming and summaries for people who were in the room do not meet that bar.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2 (Determine when human review is required)

stem: A retail marketing team uses Claude to draft about 300 product descriptions a week from supplier data sheets. The catalogue includes ordinary homewares and also supplements and children's products that carry regulated safety and health claims. Reviewing every description is not feasible with the team's capacity. Which review approach best balances risk and throughput?

options.text: Skip review, since the supplier data sheets are the source and Claude only rephrases them.
options.why: Rephrasing can introduce or strengthen a claim ("supports immunity" becoming "boosts immunity"), and regulated categories cannot go out unreviewed.

options.text: Have Claude review each description against its data sheet in a second pass with a compliance checklist, and publish automatically the descriptions it marks as compliant, sending the rest to the team.
options.why: A model checking a model is a useful filter but not accountable review; for regulated claims a human must remain in the loop.

options.text: Fully review every description in a regulated category or carrying a health, safety or performance claim; sample the rest, raising the sample rate whenever errors are found.
options.why: Tiering by consequence puts human effort where the risk is, keeps throughput on low-risk items, and uses sampling feedback to adjust coverage as quality drifts.

options.text: Review every description in full before publication, and reduce the weekly volume of new products until the team can keep up with the review load.
options.why: Full review is the safest but violates the stated capacity constraint; it does not solve the problem, it shrinks the work.

explanation: When full review is infeasible, calibrate it by risk: mandatory human review for regulated, safety-related or claim-bearing outputs; sampled review for the rest, with the sample rate driven by the error rate observed. Model self-review can support, but not replace, the human tier.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2; Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations

stem: A senior financial analyst has Claude reconcile intercompany balances from two uploaded ledgers and write a memo explaining a $240,000 variance. The memo will be filed with the external auditors as part of the year-end package. The analyst can verify every figure herself and does so; all figures check out. What is the correct determination about review?

options.text: Because the analyst has personally verified all the figures, no further review is needed before filing.
options.why: Personal verifiability is one trigger for review, but an external, regulated filing is a separate trigger that applies even when the figures are correct.

options.text: Have Claude regenerate the memo in a fresh chat and treat agreement between the two versions as the second review.
options.why: A second model run is not a human reviewer and carries no accountability; it cannot substitute for the controller's sign-off.

options.text: Add a note that the memo was prepared with AI assistance so the auditors can apply extra scrutiny themselves.
options.why: Disclosure may be appropriate, but it pushes the firm's own review obligation onto the auditors rather than meeting it.

options.text: Her verification of the figures is necessary but not sufficient; the memo still goes through the standard controller review and sign-off because it is an external, regulated record.
options.why: Two independent triggers apply: the person's ability to verify (satisfied) and the external, regulated, hard-to-reverse nature of the output (not waived by verification). The second still requires the organization's human review step.

explanation: Human review triggers are independent of each other. "I can verify it myself" removes one reason for review, but external, regulated, financial or irreversible outputs require the organization's normal review and accountability regardless of who checked the arithmetic.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2 (Determine when human review or additional verification is required)

stem: A SaaS support lead asked Claude to write a post-incident explanation of a two-hour outage. The output is a 600-word account aimed at engineers, full of terms like "connection pool exhaustion" and "failover lag". She now needs to send an update to customers. What is the best next step?

options.text: Send the engineering account to customers with a short apology added at the top, so that they can see the full technical detail and judge the severity for themselves.
options.why: Customers need what happened, how it affected them and what is being done, in plain language; raw technical detail obscures that and may alarm or confuse them.

options.text: Ask Claude to adapt the account for customers (plain language, impact and next steps first), then edit it herself before sending.
options.why: Adapting to the audience is exactly the refinement step; asking for the customer version and then editing keeps the message accurate, appropriate and owned by a person.

options.text: Ask Claude to shorten the account to 200 words, keeping the most important technical points, and send that version.
options.why: Shortening does not change the audience; a shorter engineering explanation is still written for engineers.

options.text: Post the engineering account on the status page and let customers ask questions if anything is unclear.
options.why: This shifts the effort of understanding onto customers instead of adapting the message to them.

explanation: Refining an output for its audience means changing content, structure and tone to fit the reader, not just trimming length. Ask Claude for the audience-specific version and then edit it yourself; the human remains the author.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2 (Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience)

stem: An operations lead asked Claude for a vendor-onboarding checklist and received a reasonable first version. She wants a better result before adopting it as the team standard. Which two practices most effectively use Claude to refine and compare outputs? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ask for two or three alternative versions organized differently (by phase, by owner, by risk), compare them against how the team will actually use the checklist, and merge the best elements.
options.why: Generating alternatives and comparing them against the intended use surfaces structures and items a single draft would not, and the person makes the choice.

options.text: State concrete criteria for a good checklist (must cover security review, contract sign-off, payment setup; one owner per item) and ask Claude to critique the current draft against them and revise.
options.why: Explicit criteria give Claude something specific to improve toward and make the revision checkable; vague requests produce vague improvements.

options.text: Reply "make it better" and repeat until the checklist stops changing.
options.why: Without criteria, Claude guesses what "better" means and the changes drift; convergence is not the same as fitness for purpose.

options.text: Ask Claude to double the number of items so nothing is missed.
options.why: Length is not quality; a bloated checklist gets skipped in practice and still may lack the items that matter.

options.text: Ask Claude to pick the best of its own versions and delete the others so the choice is made objectively.
options.why: Claude's preference is not the team's; comparison against the intended use is the person's job, and discarding alternatives loses useful material.

explanation: Two habits refine outputs reliably: ask for alternatives and compare them against the real use, and give explicit criteria for Claude to critique and revise against. Vague exhortations, more length, and letting Claude choose for you are common but weak substitutes.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2; Claude API docs — Prompt engineering (be clear and direct)

stem: A customer-service agent asks Claude to draft a reply to a customer whose order was lost in transit for the second time. The draft is apologetic but relies on phrases like "we regret any inconvenience this may have caused", and it promises a full refund plus a 20% discount on the next order, which the agent is not authorized to offer. What is the best way to refine this draft?

options.text: Send the draft as written; a generous offer is the fastest way to resolve a repeat failure and the tone is suitably apologetic.
options.why: The agent cannot commit the company to an offer outside his authority, and the generic phrasing will read as boilerplate to an already frustrated customer.

options.text: Ask Claude to make the reply "warmer and more human" and to drop the corporate phrases, then send the revised version as soon as it reads naturally.
options.why: Tone adjustment does not remove the unauthorized commitment, and the model still has no knowledge of what the agent can offer.

options.text: Replace the unauthorized offer with what he can actually do, make the apology specific to this customer's situation, and send it in his own words.
options.why: Refining means editing for accuracy (what is really on offer), for audience (a specific, sincere apology to a repeat-affected customer), and keeping the person as author of what goes out.

options.text: Forward the draft to a manager to approve the 20% discount and the refund, so the reply can go out unchanged once the offer is authorized.
options.why: Escalating an offer Claude invented lets the model set policy; the agent should first correct the content to the real remedy and only escalate if a bigger gesture is warranted.

explanation: A draft is raw material. Refine it by fixing content the model could not know (authority, policy, facts), tailoring it to the specific reader and situation, and sending it as your own message; do not let tone tweaks paper over commitments the sender cannot make.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2 (Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience)

stem: A program manager asked Claude for a slide outline to present a vendor-consolidation proposal. Claude produced a 14-slide outline with dense bullets and four slides of methodology. The audience is the executive committee, the slot is 15 minutes, and the purpose is a go/no-go decision on a budget request. Which two refinements best fit the audience and purpose? (Choose two.)

options.text: Restructure so the recommendation, the decision requested and the headline numbers appear on the first slide, and move the methodology to an appendix.
options.why: Executives deciding under time pressure need the ask and the evidence first; methodology supports the answer and belongs in backup material.

options.text: Keep the four methodology slides at the front so the committee sees the rigour before the recommendation.
options.why: Leading with process spends the 15 minutes on how the work was done rather than on the decision; rigour is demonstrated by having the appendix ready when asked.

options.text: Ask Claude which version it prefers and present that one.
options.why: The manager, who knows the audience and the politics, must choose; Claude's preference is not based on the room.

options.text: Reduce the font size so all 14 slides' content fits in fewer slides.
options.why: Density is the problem, not slide count; shrinking text makes the deck harder to absorb in a short slot.

options.text: Ask Claude for a second version constrained to about six slides with one message per slide, then compare it with the original against the 15-minute, decision-focused brief before choosing.
options.why: Generating a constrained alternative and comparing both against the stated audience and purpose is how refinement is done; the manager makes the final selection.

explanation: Refining for an executive audience means leading with the decision and evidence, pushing supporting detail to an appendix, and comparing alternatives against explicit constraints (time, purpose, audience). The person doing the presenting, not Claude, makes the final call.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2 (Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience)

stem: A communications manager used Claude to draft an all-hands announcement about a reorganization that the CEO will read aloud this afternoon. The structure is good, but the draft states that "no roles will be affected", which HR has not confirmed, and the voice is generic rather than the CEO's characteristically direct style. Which approach best refines the draft under these constraints?

options.text: Ask Claude to "make it sound like the CEO" and to "remove anything that isn't verified", then send the result to the CEO.
options.why: Claude has no knowledge of the CEO's voice beyond generic cues and no way to know which claims HR has confirmed; both instructions push judgement to the model that only people can exercise.

options.text: Replace the unconfirmed claim with the wording HR has approved, give Claude two or three of the CEO's past all-hands messages as style examples and ask for a revision in that voice, then edit it and have the CEO approve the final text.
options.why: The manager fixes the factual gap from the authoritative source, gives Claude concrete examples to match rather than an adjective, and keeps the human (ultimately the speaker) as author and approver.

options.text: Send the draft to the CEO as-is with a note that it was AI-generated and needs a personal pass before the meeting.
options.why: This hands an unverified claim and an off-voice draft to the busiest person with the least time; the refinement is the manager's job.

options.text: Delete the sentence about roles entirely and ask Claude to rewrite the rest in a "more executive" tone.
options.why: Removing the sentence may leave a gap employees will notice, and a vague tone instruction produces generic executive-speak rather than this CEO's voice.

explanation: Refinement combines three things: correct facts from the authoritative source (the model cannot know what is confirmed), concrete style examples rather than adjectives, and a human author and approver. Delegating verification or voice to the model with an instruction is not refinement.
reference: CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2; Claude API docs — Prompt engineering (use examples)

stem: A project manager asks Claude to write a two-page project charter that she will refine over several rounds and then share with stakeholders. Which output format is most appropriate?

options.text: An inline chat response, so the charter stays in the conversation history alongside the discussion that produced it.
options.why: A multi-section document that will be edited and shared is exactly what inline responses handle poorly; it gets buried in the chat and is awkward to iterate on.

options.text: A JSON object with a field for each section of the charter, so the structure is explicit and consistent between revisions.
options.why: JSON is for data that another tool will consume; stakeholders reading a charter need a document, not a data structure.

options.text: An artifact, so the charter is a standalone document she can edit, version and share.
options.why: Artifacts are for substantial, self-contained content that will be edited, reused or put in front of someone; a charter fits that description exactly.

options.text: A bulleted list in the chat, to keep it short enough to copy into an email.
options.why: Compressing a charter into bullets loses the content, and the copy-paste workflow is what artifacts exist to avoid.

explanation: Use an artifact for significant, self-contained content (documents, tables, slide outlines) that you will edit, reuse or share; keep quick answers inline; use structured data when a tool, not a person, is the consumer.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are artifacts and how do I use them

stem: Before a budget meeting, a marketing coordinator asks Claude to explain the difference between gross margin and contribution margin and to give a one-line example of each. Which format should she expect, and why?

options.text: A short inline answer, because it is a quick explanation she will read once and not reuse or share.
options.why: Inline is the right home for brief, conversational answers; creating a standalone document for a definition adds friction with no benefit.

options.text: An artifact, because financial definitions are reference material that should be saved as standalone documents she can return to.
options.why: Artifacts are for substantial content that will be edited or reused; a two-definition answer does not meet that bar and clutters the workspace.

options.text: A CSV table with columns for term, definition and example, so she can import it into the budget spreadsheet.
options.why: Structured data suits downstream tools; nothing here is going into a tool, and a CSV is harder for a person to read than a sentence.

options.text: A slide, because the meeting is a presentation context and the definitions may be useful to show.
options.why: The purpose is her own understanding before the meeting, not presenting; the format should follow the use, not the setting.

explanation: Match the format to how the output will be used. Quick, one-time explanations belong inline; artifacts are for content that is significant and will be reused, edited or shared; structured data is for tool consumption.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are artifacts and how do I use them

stem: A marketing analyst uploads 150 free-text customer feedback comments and asks Claude to assign each one a category and a sentiment. The results will be loaded into the team's BI dashboard, which imports spreadsheets. Which output format should she request?

options.text: A narrative summary describing the main categories and the overall mood of the feedback.
options.why: Prose cannot be imported; the dashboard needs one row per comment with consistent fields, and a summary loses the per-comment labels entirely.

options.text: An artifact containing a formatted report with a section for each category, the comments listed underneath, and a short summary of the sentiment in each section.
options.why: A report is for human reading; extracting 150 rows from headed sections back into a table is manual work the right format avoids.

options.text: Inline bullets, one per comment, with the category and sentiment written in parentheses after each so she can copy them into the dashboard.
options.why: Bullets with parenthetical labels are inconsistent and hard to parse; the dashboard import expects columns, not free text.

options.text: A CSV with fixed columns (comment id, category, sentiment), one row per comment, using a fixed set of label values.
options.why: Structured data with consistent columns and a controlled vocabulary is what downstream tools consume; it also makes the labels easy to spot-check.

explanation: When another tool is the consumer, ask for structured data: a table, CSV or JSON with fixed columns and a controlled set of values. Narrative and formatted documents are for people; they create rework when the next step is an import.
reference: Claude Help Center — Create and edit files with Claude; CCAO-F Exam Guide — Domain 2

stem: An operations lead has the transcript of a 90-minute planning meeting. She needs to circulate the decisions and action items to the 12 attendees, and she needs the action items in the team's task tracker, which imports CSV files. Which two outputs should she ask Claude for? (Choose two.)

options.text: A meeting-notes artifact containing the decisions, the action items and the open questions, organized under headings for the attendees to read and comment on.
options.why: The human-facing deliverable is a shareable document; an artifact keeps it editable and reusable rather than buried in the chat.

options.text: A CSV of the action items with columns for task, owner, due date and status, using the exact column names the tracker expects.
options.why: The tracker is a tool, so its input should be structured data matching its import schema; this avoids retyping and transcription errors.

options.text: A single long inline message containing the full summary followed by the action items, which she can copy from as needed.
options.why: Copying from a chat message into both an email and a tracker is manual, error-prone work, and the message is hard to find again later.

options.text: One artifact that includes the notes and, at the bottom, the action items written as paragraphs describing who does what by when.
options.why: Action items in prose cannot be imported; the tracker needs rows and columns, so this format forces a manual rebuild.

options.text: A JSON file of the whole meeting, including the notes, for the attendees to read.
options.why: JSON is for tools, not readers; attendees would struggle to read it and the tracker in question imports CSV, not JSON.

explanation: One source can require two formats: a document (artifact) for the people who will read and discuss it, and structured data (CSV with the consumer's column names) for the tool that will ingest it. Choosing by consumer avoids re-keying and lost content.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are artifacts and how do I use them; Create and edit files with Claude

stem: A consultant has accumulated about 30 pages of material across several chats for a client's market-entry study: Claude summaries, research-mode findings with citations, and her own notes. The client wants a report they will continue editing in their own tools, plus a competitor comparison their analysts will filter and sort in a spreadsheet. Some of the 30 pages are superseded or duplicated. Which approach best organizes and delivers this?

options.text: Paste all the material into one chat and ask Claude for a single, comprehensive artifact that contains the report, the comparison table and the source notes, so nothing is separated.
options.why: Bundling everything into one artifact carries the duplicates forward and traps the comparison in a document, so the analysts cannot filter it in their spreadsheet.

options.text: Ask Claude to strip the citations so the report reads cleanly, and embed the comparison as an image so its formatting cannot be broken when the client edits the document.
options.why: Removing citations destroys the client's ability to verify claims, and an image of a table is unusable for filtering or sorting.

options.text: Have Claude flag superseded and duplicate content for her to confirm, then produce a report artifact organized by the study's sections with sources retained, and a separate spreadsheet with one row per competitor and consistent columns.
options.why: Curation removes noise before it is formalized, the report is delivered as an editable document with provenance, and the comparison is delivered as structured data suited to the analysts' tool; each deliverable matches its consumer.

options.text: Export every chat and hand the client the transcripts so nothing is lost, and let their analysts extract the report and the comparison themselves.
options.why: This delivers raw working material rather than a curated result, shifts the organizing work onto the client, and provides no structured comparison.

explanation: Organizing and curating means pruning superseded material (with the human confirming what is dropped), preserving provenance, and delivering each part in the format its consumer needs: an editable document for the report and structured data for the table. One monolithic output or raw transcripts serve neither audience.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are artifacts and how do I use them; Create and edit files with Claude; Using Research on Claude.ai
